original_question: For which domains is the Bergman kernel function K(z,w) nonvanishing everywhere, as in the Lu Qi-Keng problem?
target_in_paper: the unnumbered Lu Qi-Keng / Bergman-kernel characterization problem in the problem-list paper arXiv:math/9509202
correct_elements: The draft correctly identifies the central object (the Bergman kernel K(z,w)), the zero-free/nonvanishing condition, and the fact that the intended topic is the Lu Qi-Keng problem.
missing_details: Specify that one is asking about a domain Ω in complex Euclidean space, typically a bounded domain Ω ⊂ ℂ^n in the classical Lu Qi-Keng setting.
Specify that K means the Bergman kernel K_Ω associated to Ω, not an arbitrary kernel.
State the full quantifier: K_Ω(z,w) ≠ 0 for every pair (z,w) ∈ Ω × Ω, not merely on the diagonal.
Make clear that the task is to characterize/classify such domains, not just to ask for examples.
Include the standard term 'Lu Qi-Keng domain' to make the question immediately recognizable and stand-alone.

No polynomial-algebra data such as ambient ring, homogeneity, degree, nilpotency, or 'for all sufficiently large m' belong to this paper/problem; those are irrelevant here and come from a mismatched template rather than arXiv:math/9509202.
refined_question: Characterize the bounded domains Ω ⊂ ℂ^n whose Bergman kernel K_Ω(z,w) is zero-free on Ω × Ω; that is, determine for which domains one has K_Ω(z,w) ≠ 0 for all z,w ∈ Ω (equivalently, which bounded domains are Lu Qi-Keng domains).
justification: arXiv:math/9509202 is a several-complex-variables problem-list paper, so the relevant target is an unnumbered Bergman-kernel/Lu Qi-Keng item rather than a numbered conjecture-theorem package. Your draft is pointed at the right classical problem, but it is not yet fully stand-alone: it omits the ambient setting Ω ⊂ ℂ^n, boundedness, the dependence of the kernel on Ω, the quantifier over all pairs (z,w), and the standard classification wording. I therefore sharpened it to the standard zero-free Bergman-kernel characterization problem and kept it broad, without narrowing it to later special subclasses such as planar, convex, or topologically trivial domains.
